text: A tag is a simple key-value pair attached to an AWS resource — Environment: Production, Team: Platform. Tags don't change how a resource behaves, they're pure metadata, used to organize resources and to track what each one actually costs. A flat list of forty untagged instances is unmanageable the moment you need to answer which ones are production, or which team owns this bill.

aws ec2 create-tags takes one or more resource IDs and one or more Key equals Value pairs, and applies all of them at once. You can pass several resource IDs in a single call, which is how a script tags a whole batch of instances in one pass instead of calling create-tags once per resource.

Tagging after the fact works, but it's easy to forget. aws ec2 run-instances accepts tags as part of the same command that creates the instance, through --tag-specifications, so nothing is ever left untagged, even briefly, between creation and your next tagging pass.

Once resources are tagged, the same describe commands from Lesson 18 can filter on them. --filters "Name=tag:Environment,Value=Production" tells describe-instances to return only instances carrying that exact tag, before --query ever reshapes the result — exactly how you'd answer "list every production instance" without scanning the whole account by eye.

A tag only shows up as its own line in Cost Explorer once it's activated as a Cost Allocation Tag, a separate manual step in AWS Billing. AWS-generated tags, prefixed aws:, are created automatically and need no activation. User-defined tags, the ones you create yourself, do need that manual step, and it can take up to 24 hours after activation before costs start appearing broken out by that tag.

Tags and cost tracking close out this chapter's CLI and automation basics — configuring the CLI, running commands against real services, CloudShell, and now tagging for both organization and billing. Chapter 6 shifts to monitoring what's actually running, starting with CloudWatch metrics and dashboards.
